doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Advice for a young pianist who wants a music career
summary: Weber answers Rowe about a high school student: you must love it and give up everything, but you never know who breaks through.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I have a student who is a very good piano player in high school. And I struggle with advising him. He wants to go into music. Now I don’t think he has the innate ability to be the next Bill Evans or that kind of thing. But I think he could make a living in the music business. And I guess I’m not sure what to tell him. Do you have advice for young musicians, how to get ahead?

What’s motivating him to play right now? I mean if someone has, I mean some musicians come from a place where they have stage mothers or fathers who will go on to be the next American Idol. And other kids, they can’t even help it, they just love to play so much that they’re naturally inclined to do it and they’re brave enough to pursue it and to have the attention span to do it for hours and hours a day. So I’m assuming he’s a young gentleman. If he has the interest in doing it all the time and is willing to give up everything — I hear this sometimes from wealthy folks who will come along and say, “you know I was a lawyer, a doctor all my life, and I’d give anything to do what you do.” Guess what? You do have to give up everything. Look at me. I mean I’m not — this is not Fort Knox. And that’s the way it is. And if your student is ready for this, that it’s not © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
going to be necessarily — who knows, maybe he will be the next big thing, maybe he’ll stumble on some thing and really get into it. It sounds like he’s into it already.

Yeah. He is, that’s his situation. He loves to play. It’s sort of ironic now that to pursue that likely you have to give up everything. First, most people have to go pay fifty grand to go to Berklee every year. You know, the investment, to put into it to get to that place where you’re not going to be rich is a dichotomy of some —

Although there is that one lucky person who breaks through and you never know who it’s going to be. Sometimes the nerdy kid with the horned-rimmed glasses ends up — I’m not saying that’s your student — but I’m saying the least likely to succeed — I don’t even remember this kid in high school — ten thousand bucks a gig? Jeez, what happened? It could happen you know. You never know what the next big thing is going to be and you never know if they come up — who knows? Thelonious Monk I’m certain was not thought to be the next Art Tatum in his day. They probably thought he doesn’t sound like him, but he carved out his own thing. And it was extraordinary in its own way. You never know what you’re going to get and that’s the beauty of jazz anyway. You never know what you’re going to get from moment to moment or over the course of your lifetime.
